title: PAM Private Markets Leaders Forum 2026
gist: A promotional Oxford Economics event/landing page for the PAM Private Markets Leaders Forum 2026, bundling teasers for four of its reports: a widening US budget deficit in 2026 driven by tariffs and tax cuts, AI-driven sticky inflation delaying Fed rate cuts to December, a one-year check-in on its 'world of self-interest' policy thesis, and an assessment of how the US-Israel-Iran conflict has and hasn't changed the geopolitical narrative.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects the improvement in the US budget deficit to fade as 2026 progresses, with tariff policies and tax cuts widening the deficit and raising concerns about future revenue growth.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A re-widening deficit narrative into 2026 argues for watching Treasury issuance and rate-sensitive assets as fiscal concerns resurface after a period of improvement.
insights.quote: The budget deficit is set to widen in 2026, influenced by tariff policies and tax cuts, raising concerns about future revenue growth.
insights.locator: Improvement in the US deficit will fade as 2026 unfolds

insights.claim: Oxford Economics attributes sticky US inflation to an AI-driven economic boom, and now expects the Federal Reserve to hold rates for longer with the next rate cut pushed to December.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A delayed Fed cut tied to AI-fueled growth suggests investors should reprice rate-cut-timing bets and watch AI capex/spending data as a driver of the inflation path.
insights.quote: A firmer economy and stickier inflation will keep the Federal Reserve on a prolonged hold – we now expect the next rate cut in December,…
insights.locator: AI boom will keep US inflation sticky

insights.claim: One year after introducing its 'world of self-interest' thesis, Oxford Economics is reassessing how global economic policy, trade, and markets have evolved under that framework and what it implies going forward.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Signals an ongoing analytical framework treating nationalist/self-interested policymaking as a persistent, multi-year macro regime rather than a one-off shock, worth tracking across trade and market outcomes.
insights.quote: A year after our “world of self-interest” thesis, we examine how global economic policy, trade, and markets have evolved and what comes next.
insights.locator: How self-Interest is reshaping global economic policy: One year on

insights.claim: Oxford Economics views the US-Israel war with Iran as reinforcing its existing long-standing geopolitical narrative, while still altering some specific elements of that narrative.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Suggests the firm's base-case geopolitical risk framework remains largely intact post-conflict, implying limited need for wholesale repositioning but attention to the specific chapters that did change.
insights.quote: The US-Israel war with Iran reinforces a long-standing narrative but rewrites a few key chapters.
insights.locator: What the Middle East conflict has changed, and what it hasn’t
